edges.description: Deficient mature C24 bile acid synthesis alters biliary composition, which is the established route to gallstone formation. The intermediate step is known in general bile acid physiology but has not been measured in AMACR deficiency specifically.
Dietary phytol is the source of the pristanic and phytanic acid that accumulate behind the enzymatic block, so intake sets the size of the accumulating pool.
edges.source: Dietary phytol and phytanic acid intake

edges.description: Pristanic and phytanic acid accumulate in Amacr-null mouse liver on a phytol diet, reproducing the human metabolite profile.
edges.limitations: Accumulation requires dietary provocation. On standard chow the null mouse does not accumulate enough to be ill, whereas patients on an ordinary human diet do - so the quantitative relationship between intake and accumulation differs between species even though the qualitative mechanism transfers.

edges.description: Phytol-fed Amacr-null mice develop liver failure as the main cause of death, with inflammation, fibrosis, necrosis, Kupffer cell proliferation and fatty change on histology, plus confirmatory serum changes.
edges.limitations: The mouse liver phenotype is fulminant and fatal within 36 weeks under dietary provocation; the human childhood phenotype is usually raised transaminases in a child who may be otherwise asymptomatic. Severity and tempo differ substantially even though the target organ agrees.

edges.description: The defining human adult phenotype is a sensorimotor neuropathy. The phytol-fed Amacr-null mouse dies of liver failure; the reported extrahepatic findings are kidney and brain abnormalities, and no peripheral neuropathy is described. The model does not reproduce the phenotype the disease was originally defined by.
edges.limitations: Because the mouse dies of hepatic failure within 36 weeks of provocation, it may simply not survive long enough for a chronic neuropathy to develop - so this is a failure to demonstrate the phenotype under the only conditions that make the mouse ill, not proof that murine nerve is spared. Either way, this model cannot currently be used to study the neuropathy or to test interventions against it.

nodes.description: A whole-gene lesion rather than a point variant: a chromosome 5p13.3 deletion spanning five genes including AMACR, homozygous in two siblings. A distinct mechanism class - the enzyme is absent rather than misfolded or catalytically dead - and it is the reason this entry leaves allele_type and zygosity unset on the pathophysiology node. The contiguous-gene span also means phenotype in these siblings cannot be attributed to AMACR alone; the index sibling came to attention through oculocutaneous albinism.

evidence.snippet: In all three patients we discovered a deficiency of alpha-methylacyl-CoA racemase (AMACR).

nodes.description: Biallelic AMACR variants abolish alpha-methylacyl-CoA racemase activity. The enzyme interconverts the (R)- and (S)-stereoisomers at the 2-methyl (or 25-methyl) position of branched-chain acyl-CoA esters. Peroxisomal beta-oxidation is stereospecific and accepts only the (S)-form, so the racemase is an obligatory gate rather than an accessory step - which is why a single enzyme loss blocks two unrelated substrate streams.

evidence.reference_title: Mutations in the gene encoding peroxisomal alpha-methylacyl-CoA racemase cause adult-onset sensory motor neuropathy.
evidence.snippet: This enzyme is responsible for the conversion of pristanoyl-CoA and C27-bile acyl-CoAs to their (S)-stereoisomers, which are the only stereoisomers that can be degraded via peroxisomal beta-oxidation.

genetic_context.description: Biallelic, but not uniformly homozygous point variants: of the 12 cohort patients, three were compound heterozygous and two siblings carried a whole-gene deletion from a 5p13.3 chromosomal deletion. ZygosityEnum is single-valued and has no "biallelic" member, and allele_type: VARIANT would not describe the deletion patients, so both slots are deliberately left unset rather than narrowed to the majority case.

nodes.description: The unusual feature of this model is that the genotype alone is not a disease. Amacr-null mice are clinically symptomless on standard laboratory chow; the phenotype has to be provoked with dietary phytol, after which all null animals died within 36 weeks while wild-types survived. It is therefore a model of the gene-environment interaction rather than of the gene, and it is the cleanest available demonstration that the substrate load driving this disease is dietary.
Ataxia, among the most frequent neurological signs in the adult natural-history cohort, developing after age 40.

evidence.reference_title: Redefining the phenotype of alpha-methylacyl-CoA racemase (AMACR) deficiency
evidence.snippet: All adult patients subsequently developed neurological signs and symptoms after the age of 40 years; most frequently neuropathy, ataxia and cognitive decline with prior normal cognitive functioning.

nodes.description: With no (S)-stereoisomer available, peroxisomal beta-oxidation of 2-methyl-branched substrates stops. The block is upstream of two independent downstream streams that share nothing but this enzyme.
nodes.id: Blocked Peroxisomal Beta-Oxidation of Branched-Chain Substrates

evidence.reference_title: Phytol is lethal for Amacr-deficient mice.
evidence.snippet: α-Methylacyl-CoA racemase (Amacr) catalyzes the racemization of the 25-methyl group in C27-intermediates in bile acid synthesis and in methyl-branched fatty acids such as pristanic acid, a metabolite derived from phytol.

nodes.description: DHCA and THCA, the C27 precursors of the mature C24 bile acids, cannot be shortened and accumulate, along with a C29-dicarboxylic acid. The accumulating intermediates are hepatotoxic and mature bile acid synthesis is deficient, which is the basis both for the liver phenotype and for treating with cholic acid.

evidence.snippet: Elevated C27-bile acid intermediates, C29-dicarboxylic acid, and pristanic acid were observed in all AMACR patients.

nodes.description: Cholestatic jaundice in the childhood presentation. Explicitly qualified as "with or without" in the review's diagnostic recommendation, so it is not obligate.

nodes.description: Pristanic acid derives from dietary phytol, largely via phytanic acid in dairy fat and ruminant meat, so the substrate driving the neurological arm of this disease is eaten rather than made. Dietary modification is recommended on that basis. The mouse model makes the dependence unusually explicit: Amacr-null mice are clinically normal on standard chow and die within 36 weeks on phytol-enriched chow, so in that model the genotype alone is not sufficient to produce disease.

nodes.description: Cholelithiasis in 2 of 12 patients, both requiring cholecystectomy - at around age 40 and, strikingly, age 15. Expected given deficient mature bile acid synthesis, and worth modelling because juvenile cholelithiasis is an unusual enough finding to be a diagnostic prompt on its own.

evidence.snippet: Two patients had a history of cholecystectomy due to gallstones (patient 4 and 6, respectively around age 40 and 15 years).

nodes.description: Liver fibrosis in 1 of 12 cohort patients, under a surveillance programme in which all patients had regular abdominal ultrasound and most had FibroScan - so this is a screened rate rather than a clinically apparent one. None of the three children showed fibrosis, consistent with it being a consequence of chronic rather than acute hepatic injury. Cirrhosis is modelled at the mechanism node but is deliberately not curated as a phenotype: the cohort reports the fibrosis-cirrhosis-HCC risk as a surveillance rationale, and no cohort patient is reported as cirrhotic.

nodes.description: The childhood presentation. Persistently elevated liver enzymes, with or without cholestatic jaundice, and coagulopathy - which in a child is the combination the review argues should trigger measurement of peroxisomal metabolites. Some children are otherwise entirely asymptomatic and come to attention only through incidental blood tests.

nodes.description: The tissue-level lesion behind the classic adult presentation. It is a diagnostic mimic: of the first two adult patients, one had pigmentary retinopathy suggesting Refsum disease and the other upper motor neuron signs suggesting adrenomyeloneuropathy - and both of those differentials are themselves disorders of branched-chain fatty acid handling, so the confusion is mechanistically principled rather than superficial.

evidence.reference_title: Mutations in the gene encoding peroxisomal alpha-methylacyl-CoA racemase cause adult-onset sensory motor neuropathy.
evidence.snippet: Two of the patients suffered from adult-onset sensory motor neuropathy. One patient also had pigmentary retinopathy, suggesting Refsum disease, whereas the other patient had upper motor neuron signs in the legs, suggesting adrenomyeloneuropathy.

nodes.description: Pristanic acid accumulates, with phytanic acid alongside it. Both derive from dietary phytol, so this arm of the disease is the one with an exogenous input - which is what makes dietary restriction plausible as therapy and what the mouse model demonstrates most sharply.

nodes.description: Episodic neurological decompensation - dysphasia, headache, sensory disturbance - that resembles neither migraine nor epilepsy nor TIA, and which in the oldest reported patient was investigated for mitochondrial disease for eight years before whole genome sequencing gave the answer. Escalation to febrile encephalopathy with coma is described.

evidence.snippet: After eight years of symptoms, she developed a febrile encephalopathy with hemispheric dysfunction, focal convulsive seizures and coma.

nodes.description: The retinal arm, which the natural-history cohort makes the leading adult presentation: retinitis pigmentosa in 5 of 9 adults, at a median age of 45, typically decades before the neurological features. Modelled downstream of the phytanic/pristanic accumulation because the same accumulation causes retinopathy in Refsum disease - but the mechanism has not been demonstrated in AMACR deficiency specifically, hence the unknown intermediates.

nodes.description: Present in one of the two original adult patients, where it suggested Refsum disease - both disorders accumulate phytanic acid, so the retinopathy is a shared consequence rather than a coincidental overlap. The natural-history cohort found it in 5 of 9 adults at a median age of 45, and it is typically the *first* manifestation: the median delay from diagnosing retinitis pigmentosa to diagnosing AMACR deficiency was 24 years, with a range to 33. That number is the single most actionable fact in this entry - an unexplained adult retinitis pigmentosa is a reason to measure pristanic acid.

nodes.description: A typical MRI pattern involving the thalami and the gray matter structures of the pons and midbrain, present in every adult patient in the natural-history cohort. Because it is consistent, it is a recognition cue rather than merely a finding - and it explains why these patients are so often worked up for mitochondrial disease first.

nodes.description: p.Ser52Pro. Recurrent: homozygous in three of the twelve cohort patients and present on one allele in two of the three compound heterozygotes. It is one of only two AMACR lesions that had been reported before this cohort, which is why it is the allele most often named in secondary sources - but the entry does not claim it is the commonest, since c.364C>T is homozygous in the same number of patients here.

nodes.description: p.His122Tyr. Equally recurrent - homozygous in three cohort patients, the same number as c.154T>C, and present on one allele of a compound heterozygote. Unlike c.154T>C it had not been reported before this cohort, so it is absent from the secondary sources that name Ser52Pro as the characteristic allele.
